title: Dog (Labrador retriever type)
summary: The domestic dog (Canis familiaris) in a Labrador-retriever shape: a 30 kg working gundog that hunts with its nose, hears sounds people cannot, and runs on its toes.

layers.basics: Click any part of the dog to meet it. The layer buttons peel it like the human body: coat, muscles, skeleton, organs, nerves, and heart and vessels. Almost every bone and organ has a counterpart in you, so each card says what is the same and what differs; where the human explorer has no matching card, it says so in words. The "Inside" buttons open the heart, the eye, the nose and the ear.
layers.deeper: A dog is a mammal, so it has the same plan as you: a backbone, four limbs, a four-chambered heart, lungs, a liver and a brain. The differences come from how it lives. It walks on its toes (digitigrade), so its heel is the "hock" halfway up the hind leg. It has a long nose lined with far more smell receptors than yours, big movable ears, and two kinds of colour-sensing cells in the eye instead of three. It cools itself mainly by panting, much more than by sweating. Compare with the whole human body in the same park: the two skeletons share nearly every bone.
layers.expert: The model is a Labrador-type male, 57 cm tall at the withers (the top of the shoulders) and 30 kg, inside the breed-standard ranges; six Labrador and Golden Retrievers in one 2015 gait study averaged 35 kg and 57 cm. The body is drawn to the standard's proportions (see the figure on the card "The dog's outside"): a little longer than tall, with the brisket (the breast) at the level of the elbow, half the height above the ground. Breed standards give height and weight for a type of dog, not for every dog, and dogs vary widely in size. A healthy dog's resting heart rate is about 70-120 beats a minute and its normal body temperature is about 37.5-39.2 C.

facts: ≈ 57 cm (UK Kennel Club: dogs 56-57 cm; AKC: 57-62 cm); measured on the model coat: ≈ 57 cm
7 neck, 13 chest, 7 lower back, 3 fused sacral, about 20-23 tail
≈ 67 cm from the point of the shoulder to the point of the buttock, about 1.18 times the height (AKC: equal to or slightly longer than the height); about 1.15 m from nose to tail tip
≈ 29 cm, half the height (AKC: elbow to ground equals half the height at the withers)
≈ 32 cm along its curve, very thick at the base and tapering, the "otter" tail (AKC: no longer than the hock)
open_questions: When, where and in how many events were dogs first domesticated? Genetic estimates of 20,000-40,000 years ago (Botigué 2017) are older than the oldest remains everyone accepts, and a 2022 study of 72 ancient wolf genomes found that dogs trace to eastern Eurasian wolves but that none of the ancient genomes is a direct match for their ancestors.

The oldest remains that researchers accept as dogs are about 14,000-15,000 years old (a jaw from Bonn-Oberkassel, Germany). Genetic estimates put the origin earlier, and when, where and in how many events it happened is still debated.

title: The dog's outside
summary: Skin, fur, ears, nose, eyes, claws and pads: everything you can see on the outside of the dog.

layers.basics: The coat button shows the dog as you would meet it. Click the fur, an ear, the nose, a paw pad or a claw.
layers.deeper: The skin is a waterproof, living wrapper made of layers; hair grows out of it, and the nose, pads and claws are special skin.
layers.expert: Together they handle touch, temperature, protection and scent.

facts: skin and coat, fur, ears, nose, eyes, paw pads, claws

title: The dog's skeleton
summary: A dog has about 320 bones, built on the same plan as yours but shaped for running on four legs: a long spine, 13 pairs of ribs, a shoulder blade on the side of the chest, and toes that bear the weight.

layers.basics: The skeleton holds the dog up, protects the brain, heart and lungs, and gives the muscles something to pull on. Press "Skeleton" and click a bone. Nearly every bone has a human counterpart, and the cards say which.
layers.deeper: Compared with a person: the dog has no working collarbone, so the front legs are held to the body by muscle and the shoulder blade can slide along the side of the chest, lengthening the stride. The dog walks on its toes, so its wrist (carpus) and ankle (tarsus, the hock) are halfway up the leg, not at the ground. It has more vertebrae in the chest and a long tail. In people: 206 bones; compare the human skeleton.
layers.expert: Counts differ a little between dogs: the tail vertebrae are about 20 (20-23 in the vertebral-formula table cited), and some dogs have a transitional extra lumbar vertebra. A commonly quoted total of about 320 bones depends on how many tail bones are counted and on small bones such as sesamoids.

facts: none that joins the shoulder (a vestige in muscle)

title: The dog's muscles
summary: Muscle is most of what a dog is made of by mass: sheets and spindles of fibre that pull on bones, with the biggest ones in the shoulder, back and haunch that drive running.

layers.basics: Press "Muscles" and click a muscle. The biggest muscles are in the hind legs (they push the dog forward) and along the back (they flex and straighten the spine at a gallop).
layers.deeper: Muscles are named by position and job, mostly with the same Latin names as in people. The hind legs provide most of the push, and the shoulder and neck muscles steer and carry the head. Tendons (the shiny cords) join muscle to bone and store elastic energy. In people, see the muscular system; most dog muscles are the same named muscles.
layers.expert: In this model the muscles fill the space between the skeleton and the skin. Their outlines are schematic: each muscle is drawn as the region of the body nearest to a core line that marks where that muscle runs, so their boundaries are approximate and many deeper muscles are not drawn as separate parts.

title: The dog's organs
summary: Brain, tongue, windpipe, lungs, heart, diaphragm, liver, stomach, spleen, intestines, kidneys and bladder, in the same arrangement as in a person but lying along a horizontal body.

layers.basics: Press "Organs". The chest holds the heart and lungs, a muscular sheet (the diaphragm) separates it from the belly, and the belly holds the digestive organs.
layers.deeper: A dog has the same main organs as you, though the model leaves some out (the pancreas, gall bladder, thyroid and adrenal glands). The main difference is posture: they hang from a horizontal spine, not stacked on a vertical one.
layers.expert: The positions here are typical, not measured on one animal, and the intestines are drawn as a schematic coil.

title: Skin and coat
summary: A dog's skin is a thin, tough layer topped by a double coat: stiff guard hairs over a soft undercoat, which together keep it warm and dry.

layers.basics: The skin keeps water in and germs out, senses touch, and grows hair. A Labrador's coat is short, dense and water-resistant (breed standard). Press the button to look inside the skin.
layers.deeper: Dog hairs grow in groups: one large guard hair (primary hair) and a tuft of finer hairs (secondary hairs) share one opening at the skin surface, called a compound follicle; a central hair is surrounded by about 3-15 smaller hairs (Merck Veterinary Manual). The undercoat traps air for warmth, the guard hairs shed water. Hair follows a growth cycle (growing, regressing, resting). Sweat glands that open straight onto the skin (the atrichial kind, like most human ones) exist on the paw pads only; the sweat glands that come with the hair follicles are of the apocrine kind. Some clinical evidence suggests limited sweating in dogs plays a minor part in cooling, and dogs cool mainly by panting. In people: the same layers (epidermis, dermis, hypodermis). Differences: people are almost hairless and sweat from the whole skin, dogs are furred and pant. Compare the human hair follicle. Compare human sweat glands.
layers.expert: The outer layer of the epidermis, the stratum corneum, is a barrier of dead flattened cells held together by lipids (ceramides, cholesterol and free fatty acids). Colour comes from melanin in the hair shaft; Labrador colours are black, yellow (cream to fox red) and chocolate. This model is yellow. The fur drawn on the model is a sample of short strokes, a small fraction of the real number of hairs.

facts: short, dense, weather-resistant double coat (breed standard)
one central hair with about 3-15 smaller hairs (Merck)
atrichial type on the paw pads only; apocrine type at the follicles
open_questions: Why did domestic dogs end up with so many coat types (short, curly, long, wire)? Several genes are known, but the full picture is still being worked out.

title: Fur
summary: The fur is the visible hair of the dog: long, stiff guard hairs on top of a dense, soft undercoat.

layers.basics: Each hair is a thin thread of dead cells packed with a tough protein called keratin. Guard hairs lie flat in the direction the dog is facing and shed rain; the undercoat underneath traps a layer of warm air.
layers.deeper: A hair grows from a follicle in the skin. Only the root is alive. As the cells push up, they fill with keratin, die, and form the shaft. The coat is shed and renewed in a cycle. The lean of the hairs from head to tail is why a dog's coat feels smooth stroked one way and rough the other. In people: the same kind of hair, but finer and sparser on most of the body.
layers.expert: Keratin is a family of fibrous proteins that form bundles called intermediate filaments, held together by disulfide bonds. The same proteins make claws and the outer skin.

facts: ≈ 16,000 (a real coat has far more hairs)

title: Ears (pinnae)
summary: The outer ear of a Labrador hangs down, but the same flap of cartilage can be raised and turned in many other dogs, to catch sound.

layers.basics: The ear flap, or pinna, gathers sound and funnels it into the ear canal. A dog can move its ears independently, which helps it find where a sound comes from. Press "Inside the ear" to see the canal and inner ear.
layers.deeper: Many small muscles move a dog's ear, so a dog with prick ears can swivel them toward a sound. In one comparison table dogs hear from about 67 Hz to about 45 kHz and people from about 64 Hz to about 23 kHz, both on the same cut-off criteria (the often-quoted human range is 20 Hz to 20 kHz). The range depends on how loud the test tone is: a loud enough tone can be heard outside it, and it varies with the breed and the age of the dog. Floppy ears like the Labrador's are common in domesticated animals and are thought to be a by-product of domestication (an idea that is still debated); the cartilage of the flap is the same. In people the outer ear is a smaller, fixed flap; few people can move it. The human explorer has no card for the ear yet.
layers.expert: The pinna is elastic cartilage covered in skin and hair. Sound waves are funnelled into the vertical and then horizontal parts of the ear canal to the eardrum.

facts: ≈ 67 Hz to 45 kHz (varies with breed and age, and with the loudness of the test tone)
≈ 64 Hz to 23 kHz on the same criteria (the usual round figure is 20 Hz to 20 kHz)

title: Nose (rhinarium)
summary: The bare, moist, dark tip of the nose, with a slit on each side, is where air and scent first enter.

layers.basics: The tip of a dog's nose is bare skin called the rhinarium. It is usually moist and cool, and each nostril has a slit that helps shape the air into a flow that goes to smell. Press "Inside the nose" to see where the air goes.
layers.deeper: The rhinarium is hairless, linked by a groove (the philtrum) to the upper lip, and connected through ducts to the vomeronasal organ (the organ for chemical signals). It is moist in healthy dogs and has cold-sensitive nerve endings that may help a dog sense which way the wind blows; the exact role of the wetness is still unsettled. In people: a nose with no bare moist tip; compare the human nasal airway.
layers.expert: The nose pad is black on a yellow Labrador in the breed standard, and it can be brown in chocolate dogs. Air is sniffed in short sniffs; part of it goes to the olfactory region at the back of the nasal cavity rather than straight to the lungs.

open_questions: Why is a healthy dog's nose wet? Several ideas exist (catching scent molecules, cooling, sensing wind) and none has settled the question.

title: Paw pads
summary: Each foot has a thick, hairless cushion under every toe and a big one under the middle of the foot.

layers.basics: The pads are shock absorbers and grippers. A dog walks on its toes, so the pads under the toe tips and the larger pad under the palm bear the weight.
layers.deeper: Pads are thick, tough skin over fat and connective tissue. They are the only place on a dog's body with sweat glands of the atrichial kind, which open straight onto the skin. The paws also carry a pad at the back of the wrist on the forelimb (the carpal pad). In people the soles also have thick skin and sweat glands, but people walk on the heel and whole foot.
layers.expert: The pad surface is a thick keratinised epidermis. Dogs cool mainly by panting.

facts: 4 toe pads, 1 palm pad, 1 wrist pad

title: Claws
summary: A claw is a curved horn sheath that grows over the last toe bone; dogs cannot pull them back.

layers.basics: Dogs use claws for grip and digging. They are blunt compared with a cat's and wear down on the ground.
layers.deeper: The claw grows from the last toe bone (the third phalanx) and is made of keratin, the same protein as hair and the outer skin. It grows continuously, so it must wear down or be trimmed. The dewclaw (the first toe) sits higher on the inner side of the foreleg than the other toes. People have flat nails on the same last toe bones; the human explorer has no card for nails yet.
layers.expert: The living core of the claw (the quick) has blood vessels and nerves.

title: Eye
summary: The dog's eye works like yours, with a mirror layer behind the retina that gives dogs better vision in dim light.

layers.basics: The eye is a ball of clear parts that focus light onto the retina, which turns it into signals for the brain. Press "Inside the eye" to cut it open and see the layers.
layers.deeper: The eye is the same design as the human eye: cornea, iris, lens, vitreous gel, retina. Differences: a dog has a reflective layer, the tapetum lucidum, behind the retina; a third eyelid (the nictitating membrane) that slides across the eye; only two kinds of colour-sensing cones instead of three; and a much larger set of rod cells for dim light. A dog's sharpness (acuity) is lower than a person's, about 20/75 in a common estimate. The retina has an area of higher cone density (the area centralis) but no foveal pit; in a dog the cones there are packed about as densely as at a primate fovea. In people: the same parts; people have three cone types, a fovea, and no tapetum. Compare the human retina.
layers.expert: A dog's eyes face forward, but less so than ours, so the field of view is wide with a smaller region seen by both eyes than in people. The third eyelid's gland can swell out of place in some dogs ("cherry eye").

facts: 2.2 cm (the size drawn, not measured on a real dog)

title: Skull
summary: The dog's skull has a long muzzle, a braincase at the back, and a bony arch on each side for the big chewing muscles.

layers.basics: The skull protects the brain and holds the eyes, the nose passages and the teeth. A Labrador has a broad skull with a moderately long muzzle. The long muzzle contains the nasal cavity, where the scent-sensing lining sits. Press "Inside the nose" to look into it.
layers.deeper: Same bones as a person's skull, arranged differently: the face (the muzzle) is long and sticks forward, while ours is flat and tucked under the braincase. A bony arch on each side (the zygomatic arch) leaves room for the jaw muscles, and the eye sockets are open at the side of the head. Skull shapes vary more between dog breeds than between almost any other animals. In people: the skull, 22 bones; same bones, but the human face is short and flat.
layers.expert: In the model the skull is a single solid with a hollow braincase, a nasal cavity and open eye sockets, and the 42 teeth sit in their rows so that the upper and lower crowns meet; a cut shows the hollows. The length of the skull from the back to the stop is drawn about equal to the length of the muzzle from the stop to the nose (breed standard: skull and foreface of approximately equal length). The model's lower jaw is about 16 cm from the hinge to the chin; a CT study of 146 Labrador heads gives about 15.5 cm for that distance. The sutures between the skull bones and the finer sinuses are not drawn.

title: Lower jaw (mandible)
summary: The lower jaw is a pair of long bones, joined at the chin, that hinge on the skull to open and close the mouth for biting and carrying.

layers.basics: The two halves of the lower jaw are joined at the chin. They swing on a hinge joint in front of the ear. A dog's jaw moves mainly up and down like a pair of scissors, with little sideways grinding.
layers.deeper: Each half is the same bone as the human mandible (in people the two halves fuse in the first year of life; in dogs the joint at the chin, the mandibular symphysis, is described as a fibrous or cartilage joint with only rare bony fusion, and the sources disagree on its class); the dog's is long and narrow and carries 22 teeth, with a tall flange (the coronoid process) where the strong temporalis muscle attaches. In people: the mandible; same bone, shorter, with a chin.
layers.expert: The model draws each half as a rod with a rising branch (the ramus, with the coronoid process and the condyle) and joins them at the chin; the model's jaw is about 16 cm long from the hinge to the chin (a CT reference for Labradors: about 15.5 cm), and the lower teeth sit in a ridge along the top of the body of the jaw and meet the upper teeth in a scissor bite.

title: Teeth (42)
summary: An adult dog has 42 teeth: for each side, 3 incisors, 1 canine, 4 premolars and 2 molars above, and the same with 3 molars below.

layers.basics: Dogs use their teeth to bite, cut, carry and tear, not to chew much. The long pointed teeth at the front corners are the canines; the small ones at the front are the incisors; the big sharp ones at the back of the mouth cut like scissors.
layers.deeper: The dental formula is 2 x (incisors 3/3, canines 1/1, premolars 4/4, molars 2/3) = 42. The carnassial teeth, the upper fourth premolar and the lower first molar, shear against each other like scissors to slice meat. People have 32 adult teeth with flat molars for grinding. In people: 32 adult teeth (8 incisors, 4 canines, 8 premolars, 12 molars); the same types, fewer, with flatter molars.
layers.expert: Teeth are made of enamel over dentine around a pulp cavity. Dogs are born without visible teeth and get a set of baby teeth, then replace them with the adult set. The number of molars differs: upper 2, lower 3 per side.

title: Neck vertebrae (7)
summary: Seven neck vertebrae, the same number as in people and giraffes, make a flexible neck.

layers.basics: Almost every mammal has seven neck vertebrae. The first two are special: the atlas lets the head nod and the axis lets it turn.
layers.deeper: In a dog the neck vertebrae are long and wide, so the neck is strong and mobile for carrying the head and the sniffing nose. The first (the atlas) has large wing-like sides; the second (the axis) has a long peg (the dens) that lets the head turn. In people: also 7, the same bones. Differences: the dog's neck is held forward and angled, ours is upright.
layers.expert: The model draws every vertebra separately along the neck line (7), each with a body, a spinous process and side processes; fine joints and discs are omitted.

title: Chest vertebrae (13)
summary: Thirteen vertebrae in the chest each carry a pair of ribs; people have twelve.

layers.basics: The chest vertebrae form the middle of the back and connect to the ribs. In a dog the first ones have tall spikes that rise above the shoulders; the withers are at the top of these spikes.
layers.deeper: The thoracic vertebrae number 13 in almost every dog, and tall spinous processes at the front give the muscles of the shoulders and neck something to pull on. People have 12 and an upright back. In people: 12 thoracic vertebrae; the same kind of vertebra, one fewer.
layers.expert: The spikes lean backward at the front of the series and forward near the back, with an "anticlinal" vertebra in between where they point straight up; the model draws the lean approximately.

ext.title: Vertebral formula of the dog (open-access paper, Table 2)

title: Lower-back vertebrae (7)
summary: Seven lumbar vertebrae in the loin let the dog arch and stretch its back when it runs.

layers.basics: The lower back has no ribs. Its vertebrae are large and flex at a gallop, so the back works like a spring.
layers.deeper: A dog has 7 lumbar vertebrae and a person 5. The long side wings (transverse processes) point forward and downward and carry the big back muscles. In people: 5 lumbar vertebrae, which bear the weight of an upright body; the dog's carry only the horizontal body.
layers.expert: In one study of 89 dogs, 4 (4.5 %) had a transitional or extra lumbar vertebra (a supernumerary L8, or the last lumbar vertebra fused with the sacrum).

title: Sacrum (3 fused)
summary: Three vertebrae fused into one plate join the spine to the pelvis.

layers.basics: The sacrum is the strong link between the backbone and the hip bones. The weight of the hindquarters is carried through it.
layers.deeper: A dog's sacrum has 3 fused vertebrae, a person's has 5. In people: 5 fused sacral vertebrae.
layers.expert: The sacrum joins the hip bones at the sacroiliac joints, which move very little.

ext.title: Vertebral formula of the dog (open-access paper, Table 2)

title: Tail vertebrae (about 20)
summary: About twenty small vertebrae make the tail, from big blocks at the base to slender rods at the tip.

layers.basics: The tail balances the dog when it turns, helps it swim as a rudder, and signals mood. A Labrador's "otter" tail is thick at the base and tapers.
layers.deeper: Dogs have 20-23 tail vertebrae depending on breed and tail length (about 20 here); people have a tiny tailbone of 3-5 fused vertebrae, the coccyx. The tail is moved by muscles along its sides. In people the tailbone (coccyx) is the equivalent, a few small fused bones at the end of the sacrum; the human explorer has no card for it yet.
layers.expert: Some breeds are born without a tail or with a short one; wagging is done by muscles attached to the first tail bones.

title: Ribs (13 pairs)
summary: Thirteen pairs of ribs form the dog's deep chest: nine join the breastbone, four do not.

layers.basics: The ribs protect the heart and lungs and move with each breath. A dog's chest is deep from top to bottom and narrow side to side, which suits running.
layers.deeper: Nine pairs of ribs link to the breastbone by cartilage (the true ribs), four do not (the false and floating ribs); the last is usually free. People have 12 pairs, with 7 reaching the sternum directly. In people: 12 pairs, a barrel-shaped chest that is wide from side to side.
layers.expert: The model draws the 13 pairs with their cartilage tips; their spacing and curve are typical, not measured.

title: Costal cartilages
summary: Bars of cartilage join the ribs to the breastbone and let the chest flex.

layers.basics: Each rib continues in cartilage, which is more springy than bone, so the chest expands for breathing and gives under a knock.
layers.deeper: In a dog the costal cartilages are long in the back ribs (the last true ribs and the arch), which curve forward and join the cartilage in front. In people: the same, but shorter and more uniformly spaced.
layers.expert: Costal cartilage is hyaline cartilage and often hardens (calcifies) with age.

title: Breastbone (sternum)
summary: The sternum is a row of eight small bones along the chest floor that the ribs hang from.

layers.basics: The dog's sternum is a keel at the bottom of the chest. The front end projects between the front legs; the last bone ends in a flexible tip of cartilage.
layers.deeper: The dog's sternum is made of a series of segments (sternebrae), usually eight, instead of the three fused parts in people (manubrium, body, xiphoid process). In people: three fused parts; the same function.
layers.expert: The model draws eight segments and a cartilage tip, approximate in length.

title: Pelvis
summary: The pelvis is the strong bony ring the hind legs swing from.

layers.basics: Two hip bones join the spine (through the sacrum) and meet at the bottom. The hip sockets face sideways, so the thigh swings back and forth under the body.
layers.deeper: Each hip bone is three bones fused: the ilium (a blade sloping up toward the spine), the ischium (the point you can feel at the rump) and the pubis. In people the ilium is a broad bowl; in dogs it is long and narrow. In people: the same three bones forming a bowl. Different: the dog's pelvis is long and tilted for a horizontal back.
layers.expert: The model's pelvis is a smoothed shape, not a bone-by-bone reconstruction.

title: Penis bone (baculum)
summary: Male dogs have a bone in the penis, the os penis, that stiffens it.

layers.basics: The model is a male, so it has this bone. It lies inside the penis, beneath the belly, and has a groove for the urethra.
layers.deeper: Many mammals have a baculum; people do not. In dogs it sits in the penis alongside an erectile part that swells. People have no baculum.
layers.expert: The model's shape and position are schematic: the bone is placed under the abdomen, near where it would lie in the sheath.

facts: male dogs and many other mammals

title: Shoulder blade (scapula)
summary: The shoulder blade lies flat on the side of the chest and is held on by muscle only.

layers.basics: A dog has no collarbone to brace the shoulder, so the shoulder blade is joined to the body only by muscles. It can swing, which lengthens the stride.
layers.deeper: Same bone as in people. A ridge (the spine of the scapula) runs along the blade; the shoulder joint is at the lower end of the blade itself, not on the ridge. In people the scapula is on the back and braced by the collarbone; in the dog it stands on the side of the chest.
layers.expert: The model draws a flat blade with a ridge. Dogs have a tiny collarbone remnant embedded in a muscle; it is not drawn.

title: Upper arm bone (humerus)
summary: The dog's upper arm bone runs from the shoulder back to the elbow, tucked close to the chest.

layers.basics: The humerus is the same bone as in your upper arm. In a dog it slopes back, so the elbow sits just behind the chest, level with the lowest point of the ribs.
layers.deeper: In people the humerus hangs down from a shoulder on the side; in the dog it is angled so the elbow is behind and the foot is below the body. In people: the same bone.
layers.expert: The model draws a shaft with rounded ends, slightly curved.

title: Forearm bones (radius and ulna)
summary: Two long bones make the forearm, and the ulna sticks out behind the elbow as a point.

layers.basics: The point of the elbow is the end of the ulna, the same bone you can feel behind your own elbow. The radius carries most of the weight in a dog.
layers.deeper: The radius and ulna are tied together by a tough ligament so the dog's forearm can twist only a little, unlike yours; the two bones act as one stiff post for running. In people: the same two bones; people can rotate the forearm (palm up or down), dogs very little.
layers.expert: The model draws the two as separate rods with an elbow point.

title: Carpus (the dog's wrist)
summary: The "knee" on a dog's front leg is its wrist, the carpus: a cluster of small bones halfway down the leg.

layers.basics: People call it the front "knee", but it is the same joint as your wrist. The dog walks on its fingertips, so the wrist is far from the ground.
layers.deeper: The carpus has seven bones in two rows, like your eight. A dog stands on the toes, not the palm, which is why the wrist is high (digitigrade stance). In people: the wrist has 8 bones, and the palm rests on the ground only when crawling.
layers.expert: The model draws seven small bones as balls; their real shapes are more irregular.

title: Metacarpals (palm bones)
summary: Four long palm bones stand almost upright, so the dog stands on its toes.

layers.basics: In you the palm bones are in the hand. In the dog they are the long straight bones in the lower foreleg, between wrist and toes.
layers.deeper: The first metacarpal (the thumb side) is short and goes with the dewclaw, the other four reach the ground. In people: five metacarpals in the palm.
layers.expert: The model draws four.

title: Toe bones
summary: Each toe has three small bones, like your fingers, and the dog stands on them.

layers.basics: The toes are what a dog's foot is made of: bones, pads and claws. The foot is arched so the weight falls on the pads.
layers.deeper: Three phalanges per toe (the last carries the claw). A forefoot has four weight-bearing toes plus the dewclaw; a hind foot has four. In people: the fingers have 3 bones, the thumb 2. In people the toes also have 3 bones (the big toe 2).
layers.expert: The model draws three bones per toe.

title: Dewclaw (first toe)
summary: The dewclaw is the dog's thumb: a small toe on the inner side of the foreleg, set higher up than the other toes.

layers.basics: It is the first toe, your thumb counterpart. It is higher up the leg than the other toes and has a claw.
layers.deeper: Forelegs carry a dewclaw; hind dewclaws are rare in a Labrador. Some are attached only by skin and are often removed in some breeds. In people: the thumb.
layers.expert: The model draws a two-bone toe with a claw.

title: Thigh bone (femur)
summary: The femur is the long bone of the thigh, sloping forward from the hip to the knee.

layers.basics: The femur is the same bone as yours. In a dog it slopes forward and down from the hip to the stifle (the dog's knee), which is at the front of the flank.
layers.deeper: Same joint: a ball at the top fits into the hip socket. The dog's femur is more angled. In people: the same bone; ours stands upright.
layers.expert: The model draws a curved shaft with rounded ends.

title: Kneecap (patella)
summary: The kneecap sits in front of the knee (the stifle) in the tendon of the big thigh muscle.

layers.basics: It acts like a pulley: the front thigh muscle pulls on it and it straightens the leg.
layers.deeper: The patella is the same bone as yours. In small dogs it can slip out of its groove. In people: the same bone.
layers.expert: The model draws a small oval bone.

title: Shin bones (tibia and fibula)
summary: The tibia carries the weight below the stifle; the thin fibula runs beside it.

layers.basics: The shin runs from the stifle down and back to the hock. The thin bone alongside is the fibula.
layers.deeper: The same pair of bones as in your lower leg. In people: the same bones.
layers.expert: The model draws the two as rods.

title: Tarsus (the hock and heel bone)
summary: The hock is the dog's ankle: the pointed bone sticking up and back is the calcaneus, the heel bone.

layers.basics: The sharp-angled joint halfway up a dog's hind leg looks like a backward knee, but it is the ankle. The pointed bone at its back is your heel bone. The dog walks on its toes, so the heel is high above the ground.
layers.deeper: The tarsus is made of seven bones like yours. The calcaneus is long and forms a lever for the calf muscle (via the calcaneal tendon, the dog's Achilles). In people: the same bones, but the heel rests on the ground.
layers.expert: The model draws all seven tarsal bones as simple shapes: the heel bone (calcaneus), the talus, a central bone and four small distal bones (the small ones are balls).

title: Metatarsals (sole bones)
summary: Long sole bones stand upright in the lower hind leg.

layers.basics: In you these are the bones of the middle of the foot. In a dog they form the long lower part of the hind leg, from hock to toes.
layers.deeper: Four long bones for the four hind toes. In people: five metatarsals.
layers.expert: The model draws four.

title: Temporalis (chewing)
summary: A fan-shaped muscle on the side of the skull that closes the jaw with great force.

layers.basics: It runs from the side of the skull to the lower jaw. When it contracts, the mouth snaps shut. It is large in dogs, which bite and hold prey.
layers.deeper: It is the same muscle as in people, where it is smaller; a dog's temporalis is a main jaw closer, and is attached to a ridge on top of the skull in some dogs. In people: the temporalis closes the jaw too, but chewing is grinding, so sideways muscles matter more; the human explorer has no card for the chewing muscles yet.
layers.expert: The outline drawn in the model is schematic: it shows the region of the body that this muscle occupies, not its exact edges, and many muscles lie under the ones shown.

title: Masseter (chewing)
summary: The muscle of the cheek that closes the jaw.

layers.basics: It runs from the cheekbone to the angle of the lower jaw. Together with the temporalis it provides the bite force.
layers.deeper: The same muscle as in people. In dogs it works with the temporalis for a strong shear and crush. In people: also the masseter; the human explorer has no card for it yet.
layers.expert: The outline drawn in the model is schematic: it shows the region of the body that this muscle occupies, not its exact edges, and many muscles lie under the ones shown.

title: Muscles of the muzzle and lips
summary: Thin muscles that move the lips and nose and make a dog's expressions.

layers.basics: They pull the lips back for a snarl or a smile, wrinkle the nose and move the whiskers.
layers.deeper: People have muscles of facial expression, too; dogs use theirs mainly to signal, with the lips, ears and eyebrows. In people: the muscles of facial expression, in the same place but more finely controlled. The human explorer has no card for them yet.
layers.expert: The outline drawn in the model is schematic: it shows the region of the body that this muscle occupies, not its exact edges, and many muscles lie under the ones shown.

title: Splenius and neck extensors
summary: Muscles along the top of the neck that lift and turn the head.

layers.basics: They run from the neck and the top of the shoulders up to the back of the skull. They hold up the dog's head.
layers.deeper: A dog's head is carried in front of the body, so these muscles are strong and thick. In people the equivalent neck extensors (such as the splenius) are smaller, since the head balances on top of the spine; the human explorer has no card for them yet.
layers.expert: The outline drawn in the model is schematic: it shows the region of the body that this muscle occupies, not its exact edges, and many muscles lie under the ones shown.

title: Brachiocephalicus (draws the foreleg forward)
summary: A strap of muscle from the head and neck to the upper arm that pulls the foreleg forward and turns the head.

layers.basics: When the foot is planted it turns or tips the neck. When the head is fixed it swings the leg forward, lengthening the stride.
layers.deeper: It is not special to dogs: it is found in dogs and other animals that have no working collarbone, where it joins the neck and head to the arm. A thin remnant of the collarbone lies in a faint line across the muscle, the clavicular intersection: in a study of 50 adult dogs of 10 breeds the clavicle had ossified in 96 %, attached to this intersection. In people: no single equivalent. The part to the arm (the cleidobrachialis) is counted as the clavicular part of the deltoid, and the part to the head compares with the collarbone head of the sternocleidomastoid; the human explorer has cards for the deltoid and the sternocleidomastoid.
layers.expert: The outline drawn in the model is schematic: it shows the region of the body that this muscle occupies, not its exact edges, and many muscles lie under the ones shown.

title: Sternocephalicus and neck flexors
summary: Muscles along the underside of the neck that nod and turn the head.

layers.basics: They connect the breastbone to the skull and pull the head down and sideways.
layers.deeper: The sternocephalicus corresponds to the human sternocleidomastoid. In people: the sternocleidomastoid does a similar job.
layers.expert: The outline drawn in the model is schematic: it shows the region of the body that this muscle occupies, not its exact edges, and many muscles lie under the ones shown.

title: Trapezius
summary: A flat triangular muscle on the shoulders and withers that pulls the shoulder blade toward the spine.

layers.basics: It holds the shoulder blade to the body and helps lift the foreleg and the neck.
layers.deeper: The dog trapezius has a neck part and a chest part. It is the same muscle as in people. In people: also the trapezius, which shrugs the shoulders.
layers.expert: The outline drawn in the model is schematic: it shows the region of the body that this muscle occupies, not its exact edges, and many muscles lie under the ones shown.

title: Latissimus dorsi
summary: A broad sheet over the ribs that pulls the foreleg back.

layers.basics: It runs from the back to the upper arm. When it contracts, the foreleg is drawn back, as at the end of each stride.
layers.deeper: It is the same muscle as in people, where it pulls the arm down and back. In people: the latissimus dorsi, which pulls the arm down in swimming and pull-ups.
layers.expert: The outline drawn in the model is schematic: it shows the region of the body that this muscle occupies, not its exact edges, and many muscles lie under the ones shown.

title: Serratus ventralis and the chest wall (intercostal muscles)
summary: Muscles over the ribs: one sheet slings the trunk between the shoulder blades, and the small ones between the ribs move the ribs when breathing.

layers.basics: The serratus ventralis hangs the body between the two shoulder blades, like a hammock, because there is no collarbone to hold the front legs. The small muscles between the ribs help breathe.
layers.deeper: In people the serratus anterior keeps the shoulder blade on the back. The intercostals are the same. In people: the intercostal muscles move the ribs as well, but the serratus anterior is smaller; the human explorer has no card for them yet.

title: Pectoral muscles
summary: Muscles on the front of the chest that pull the foreleg in toward the body.

layers.basics: They run from the breastbone to the upper arm and carry weight and pull the legs inward.
layers.deeper: Dog pectorals are in two layers (superficial and deep). They are homologous to the human pectoralis muscles. In people: the pectoralis major.
layers.expert: The outline drawn in the model is schematic: it shows the region of the body that this muscle occupies, not its exact edges, and many muscles lie under the ones shown.

title: Longissimus and the back extensors
summary: The long muscles on either side of the spine that stretch the back and lift the head.

layers.basics: They run the whole length of the back, over the vertebrae. They straighten the back when the dog leaps or runs.
layers.deeper: These are the epaxial muscles, the same group as the erector spinae of the human back. In people: the erector spinae along the spine; the human explorer has no card for them yet.
layers.expert: The outline drawn in the model is schematic: it shows the region of the body that this muscle occupies, not its exact edges, and many muscles lie under the ones shown.

title: External oblique (flank)
summary: A broad sheet of muscle in the flank that tightens the belly.

layers.basics: It holds the belly in, bends the trunk and helps breathing out.
layers.deeper: It is the dog's outermost belly muscle, the same one as in people. In people: the external obliques, one of the abdominal muscles.
layers.expert: The outline drawn in the model is schematic: it shows the region of the body that this muscle occupies, not its exact edges, and many muscles lie under the ones shown.

title: Rectus abdominis
summary: A pair of straps of muscle along the underside of the belly.

layers.basics: It runs from the ribs to the pelvis and flexes the back, as in a person's "six-pack".
layers.deeper: In dogs the rectus abdominis lies on the belly floor and arches the back when the hind legs swing forward. In people: the rectus abdominis, the same name and position.

title: Supraspinatus and infraspinatus (shoulder)

layers.deeper: They are the dog's flexors, as in your forearm. In people: the forearm flexors.

summary: Below the wrist there is little muscle, only cords of tendon that run to the toes.

layers.basics: The long tendons pull the toes. They also store spring energy when the paw lands.

layers.basics: They run from the pelvis to the thigh bone. They are the main drive of the hind leg.
layers.deeper: The middle gluteal muscle (gluteus medius) is the largest in a dog; it corresponds to the same muscle in people. In people: the gluteus maximus is the largest and the other gluteals are smaller.

title: Brain
summary: The dog's brain does what yours does, and it devotes a larger share to smell: its olfactory bulbs are big.

layers.basics: The brain is the control centre. It processes signals from the senses, remembers, decides and sends orders to muscles. A dog's brain sits behind the muzzle and above the throat, inside the braincase.
layers.deeper: It has the same main parts as the human brain: two cerebral hemispheres, a cerebellum behind them and a brainstem. The surface is folded, but less than a human's. The part that processes smell (the olfactory bulb) is large in the dog; the parts for planning and language are smaller. In people: the same organ in the same layout; larger, more folded, and with a large frontal lobe. Compare the human cerebellum.
layers.expert: The model is built from a typical shape of the brain; its size, folds and relative proportions are approximate.

open_questions: How much does a dog understand of what it hears and sees? Research on dog cognition is active and unsettled.

title: Olfactory bulbs
summary: Two bulbs at the front of the brain take in the signals from the nose and sort them by smell.

layers.basics: Every smell receptor cell in the nose sends a thread to a bulb. In a dog the bulbs sit at the front of the brain, ahead of the hemispheres, and look like two big knobs.
layers.deeper: In the bulb, receptor cells of one kind send their threads to the same small clusters (glomeruli), so each cluster responds to one kind of smell molecule. From the bulb the signal goes to the brain. In people: the same two bulbs, on the underside of the frontal lobes, smaller relative to the brain.
layers.expert: A dog's olfactory bulbs are proportionally larger than a person's. But the human bulb is large in absolute terms and holds a similar number of neurons to the bulbs of other mammals (McGann 2017, a review), so the dog's better sense of smell is not explained by bulb size alone. The number of receptor genes and cells, the area of the lining and what the rest of the brain does with the signal all matter, and how much each contributes is debated.

open_questions: Is a dog's better sense of smell down to its bulbs, its receptors, or how the brain interprets the signal? The answer is not settled.

title: Tongue
summary: The dog's tongue laps water, helps it taste, and cools it by exposing a wet surface to air as it pants.

layers.basics: The tongue is a muscle. A dog curls its tongue back to scoop water, and lolls it out to pant. Press "Cut in half" to see it inside the mouth.
layers.deeper: It is a muscular organ like yours, covered with taste buds and papillae. Panting moves air over the wet tongue and the moist lining of the mouth and nose; this is how dogs cool themselves, because sweating plays at most a minor part (the sweat glands that open on the skin are only on the pads). In people: the same muscular organ with taste buds; people cool by sweating, not by exposing the tongue.
layers.expert: The surface of a dog's tongue is rough with tiny projections (papillae). The tongue is also a cooling radiator: blood flow to it rises when the dog is hot.

title: Larynx
summary: The voice box at the top of the windpipe, which the dog uses to bark, growl and whine.

layers.basics: The larynx sits at the throat. It closes when the dog swallows so food does not go down the windpipe, and its vocal folds vibrate to make sound.
layers.deeper: It is made of cartilages, like yours. A dog barks by passing air over the vocal folds, with the sound shaped by the throat and mouth. In people: the same organ, lower in the neck.
layers.expert: The model draws a simplified shape.

title: Windpipe (trachea)
summary: A flexible tube reinforced by C-shaped rings of cartilage carries air from the throat to the lungs.

layers.basics: The windpipe runs down the front of the neck, over the heart, and splits into two main bronchi, one to each lung. The rings keep it open.
layers.deeper: It has the same design as the human windpipe: C-shaped rings of cartilage with a soft muscle strip on the back. The number of rings varies from dog to dog.
layers.expert: The model draws 35 rings, a typical-looking number, not a measured one.

title: Main bronchi
summary: The windpipe divides into a left and a right bronchus, and they branch again and again inside the lungs.

layers.basics: Each bronchus carries air into one lung. Inside the lung it divides into smaller and smaller tubes.
layers.deeper: The same branching airway as in people, ending in tiny air sacs (alveoli). In people: the same two bronchi.
layers.expert: The model draws only the two main bronchi.

title: Gullet (esophagus)
summary: The gullet is the muscular tube that carries swallowed food from the throat to the stomach.

layers.basics: It runs down the neck beside the windpipe, through the chest and through the diaphragm. Waves of muscle push the food along.
layers.deeper: The same organ as in people. It lies on the left of the windpipe at the base of the neck. In people: the same tube.
layers.expert: The model draws a simple tube.

title: Lungs
summary: The lungs fill the chest on either side of the heart; they take oxygen from the air into the blood.

layers.basics: Air goes in and out through the windpipe. In the lungs it reaches millions of tiny air sacs, where oxygen passes into the blood and carbon dioxide passes out. A dog's breathing rate at rest is about 18-34 breaths a minute.
layers.deeper: The right lung has four lobes and the left two in most references (the model draws them as one body per side). A dog pants to cool down: fast, shallow breaths move air over the wet tongue and nose rather than deep into the lungs. In people: the same organs; the left lung has two lobes and the right three, with a notch for the heart in the left.
layers.expert: Resting breathing is 18-34 breaths a minute. The lungs are drawn semi-transparent in the Organs view so that the heart can be seen behind them.

title: Heart
summary: A dog's heart is a four-chambered pump just like yours, but it beats faster: about 70-120 times a minute at rest.

layers.basics: The heart pumps blood in two loops. The right side sends blood to the lungs to pick up oxygen; the left side sends it to the rest of the body. Press "Inside the heart" to cut it open.
layers.deeper: The structure is the same as in people: two atria (receiving rooms) and two ventricles (pumping rooms), with valves that keep the blood flowing one way. The left ventricle has the thickest wall because it pumps against the pressure of the whole body. A dog's heart weighs about 0.6-1.1% of its body mass (a study of 30 dogs), which is about 180-330 g at 30 kg. In people: the same four chambers, valves and layout; differences are the rate (60-100 per minute) and the position, because the human heart is in an upright chest.
layers.expert: The resting heart rate depends on size: large dogs near the low end, small dogs near the high end. It rises with excitement and exercise and in many dogs changes with each breath (sinus arrhythmia).

title: Diaphragm
summary: A sheet of muscle that separates the chest from the belly and drives breathing.

layers.basics: When the diaphragm tightens it flattens and pulls air into the lungs; when it relaxes it domes up and air goes out. It is shaped like a dome that bulges into the chest.
layers.deeper: The same muscle as in people. In a dog it is attached around the rib cage and to the spine, and the liver lies against its rear surface. In people: the same muscle.
layers.expert: The model draws a thin dome.

title: Liver
summary: The liver is the dog's largest internal organ: a chemical factory that cleans the blood, makes bile and stores sugar.

layers.basics: It lies just behind the diaphragm. Blood from the gut passes through it first, so it can break down toxins and store nutrients.
layers.deeper: The same organ as in people, with the same functions. Most descriptions divide the dog's liver by deep fissures into six lobes: left lateral, left medial, quadrate, right medial, right lateral and caudate (other textbooks group them differently, as four lobes with sub-lobes). In people: the same organ with the same functions, but divided differently into lobes.
layers.expert: The model draws three lobes fused, a simplification of the six real lobes; its shape and size are approximate.

facts: 6 in a dog (the model draws 3, fused)

ext.title: Hepatic veins of the dog, corrosion casts of 18 livers (Folia Morphologica 2014): the canine liver in six lobes

title: Stomach
summary: A dog's stomach is a J-shaped sac on the left that holds a big meal and starts digesting it.

layers.basics: Food passes down the gullet to the stomach, where it is mixed with acid and enzymes. A dog can eat a lot at once, and its stomach can hold from about half a litre in a small dog to several litres in a large one.
layers.deeper: It is a simple glandular stomach with three regions (fundus, body, pyloric part). People have the same design. In people: the same type of stomach.
layers.expert: Capacity ranges from about 0.5 L (small dogs) to about 8 L (large), according to the open-access paper cited.

ext.title: Gastrointestinal tract of the dog: stomach and intestine lengths (open-access paper)

title: Spleen
summary: The spleen is a long, flat organ beside the stomach that filters the blood and stores red blood cells.

layers.basics: It removes old blood cells and is part of the immune system. In the dog it is long and flat, lying along the left side of the stomach.
layers.deeper: The same organ as in people; it can hold and release a reserve of blood. In people: the same organ, smaller and fist-shaped.
layers.expert: The model draws it as a straight band; its real shape is more curved and varies with the dog.

title: Small intestine
summary: A long coiled tube where food is digested and almost all nutrients are taken into the blood.

layers.basics: The small intestine fills much of the belly in loops. Digestive juices from the liver and pancreas are added, and the walls absorb nutrients.
layers.deeper: The small intestine of a 33 kg dog is about 6.4 m long (the open-access paper, which lists 2.4 m at 5 kg). In people: the same organ.
layers.expert: The model draws a schematic coil that is much shorter than the real tube; it is not to scale.

facts: ≈ 6.4 m at 33 kg; ≈ 2.4 m at 5 kg

ext.title: Gastrointestinal tract of the dog: stomach and intestine lengths (open-access paper)

title: Large intestine and rectum
summary: The large intestine takes water from what is left and forms the stool, which leaves at the anus.

layers.basics: It starts with a small pouch, the caecum, goes forward, across and back along the roof of the belly, and ends in the rectum.
layers.deeper: The dog's large intestine is short and fairly straight. It is about 32 cm in a miniature poodle and about 99 cm in a Great Dane (open-access paper). In people: the same organ; the human colon is relatively longer.
layers.expert: The caecum in the dog is a small coil.

ext.title: Gastrointestinal tract of the dog: stomach and intestine lengths (open-access paper)

title: Kidneys
summary: The two bean-shaped kidneys, below the spine in the roof of the belly, clean the blood and make urine.

layers.basics: Blood passes through each kidney, which filters out waste and extra water. The urine goes down a tube to the bladder.
layers.deeper: The same organ as in people. The right kidney sits slightly further forward than the left. In people: the same organs; compare the human kidney.
layers.expert: The model draws two simple bean shapes.

title: Urinary bladder
summary: A stretchy bag at the back of the belly that stores urine.

layers.basics: Urine trickles down from the kidneys and collects here. When full, the bladder signals the dog to find a place to urinate.
layers.deeper: It is the same organ as in people. In the male dog, the urine leaves through the urethra, which runs through the penis. In people: the same organ.
layers.expert: The model draws a simple pear.

title: Spinal cord
summary: A cable of nerve tissue runs inside the backbone from the brain to the lower back, carrying signals both ways; nerves for the hind legs and tail leave it and run on backward.

layers.basics: The spinal cord connects the brain to the body. Nerves branch off between each pair of vertebrae. Press "Nerves" to see it.
layers.deeper: It is protected by the vertebrae. In dogs the working cord ends in the lower back, at about the junction of the sixth and seventh lumbar vertebrae, about one vertebra further back in small dogs (under 7 kg). Beyond its end the nerve roots for the hind legs and tail stream backward inside the vertebral canal as a bundle, the cauda equina. In people: the same organ, 31 pairs of nerves.
layers.expert: The cord tapers to a point (the conus medullaris) and ends in a thin thread (the filum terminale) inside a sac of the membrane around it (the dural sac), which ends further back. In an MRI study of 101 dogs the end of the cord lay further forward as the dog's body weight rose, while the end of the sac stayed at about the same place; in 48 Cavalier King Charles spaniels, a breed whose cord is known to end further back than in other dogs, it ended at the sixth lumbar vertebra in one, the seventh in 31 and in the sacrum in 15. The model draws a smooth tube of one width from the skull to the last lumbar vertebra; the real cord is thicker where the nerves for the limbs leave it, in the neck and in the lower back.

facts: lower back, about L6-L7, further forward in larger dogs

title: Nerves of the foreleg (brachial plexus)
summary: A braid of nerves from the neck and chest spine feeds each foreleg.

layers.basics: The nerves leave the spinal cord at the base of the neck, mix in a network (the plexus) in the armpit, and then run down the leg as the main nerves to the muscles and the skin of the foreleg.
layers.deeper: The brachial plexus is the same arrangement as in people. Its main branches go to the shoulder, to the elbow extensor (radial nerve) and the paw (median and ulnar nerves). In people: the same plexus feeds the arm.
layers.expert: The model draws a simplified set of the main trunks.

title: Sciatic nerve and nerves of the hindleg
summary: The big sciatic nerve runs from the lower back down the back of the thigh to the foot.

layers.basics: The nerves of the hind leg leave the lower spinal cord and join into the sciatic nerve, the thickest nerve in the body. It runs behind the hip joint and down the thigh.
layers.deeper: The same name and course as in people. In a dog it supplies the hamstring muscles, the lower leg and the foot. In people: the sciatic nerve, from the lower back down the back of the leg.
layers.expert: The model draws a simplified path.

title: Vagus nerves
summary: The vagus nerves wander from the brain through the neck to the heart, lungs and gut, and slow the heart.

layers.basics: One vagus nerve runs down each side of the neck. They carry messages that slow the heartbeat and control digestion.
layers.deeper: The same nerve as in people (cranial nerve X). In dogs, the resting heart rate varies with breathing because of vagal activity. In people: the same nerve.
layers.expert: The model draws one line per side.

title: Optic nerves
summary: Each eye is joined to the brain by an optic nerve, a cable of on the order of 100,000 or more fibres.

layers.basics: The optic nerve carries the signals from the retina to the brain. Its fibres leave the eye at a spot with no light-sensing cells (the blind spot).
layers.deeper: The same nerve as in people (cranial nerve II). In people: the same nerve.
layers.expert: The model draws a short tube from each eye.

facts: ≈ 115,000-150,000 (a range cited in a 2025 beagle paper; one older count of retinal ganglion cells gave about 81,000, so estimates differ)

ext.title: Optic nerve head area and retinal nerve fibre layer in beagles (2025 open-access paper; cites 115,000-150,000 axons in the canine optic nerve)

title: Arteries
summary: Arteries carry blood away from the heart: the aorta is the main one, and branches feed the head, legs and organs.

layers.basics: Press "Heart and vessels". The red tubes are arteries. They are thick and springy to take the pulse of each heartbeat.
layers.deeper: The big artery (the aorta) leaves the left ventricle, arches over and runs under the spine to the pelvis, where it divides to supply the hind legs. Branches to the head are called carotid arteries and to the forelegs, subclavian and brachial arteries. In people: arteries with the same structure. Compare the human aorta.
layers.expert: The model draws the main vessels only, as a schematic of the layout, not an exact map.

ext.title: Blood transfusions in animals (Merck Veterinary Manual)

title: Veins
summary: Veins carry blood back to the heart; the big ones are the vena cavae.

layers.basics: The blue tubes are veins. Blood in them has less oxygen than blood in the arteries, except in the pulmonary veins from the lungs.
layers.deeper: The cranial vena cava collects blood from the head and forelegs and the caudal vena cava collects blood from the rest of the body. The jugular veins in the neck are where blood is often drawn. In people: the same. Compare the human vena cava.
layers.expert: The model draws the main trunks only.

facts: cranial and caudal vena cava, jugulars

title: Left ventricle
summary: The strong pump of the left side: it pushes blood out through the aorta to the whole body.

layers.basics: This chamber is shown cut open in the "Inside the heart" view: red for oxygen-rich blood, blue for oxygen-poor.
layers.deeper: Its wall is thicker than that of the right ventricle because it pumps against the pressure of the whole body. The layout is the same as in people. In people: the same chamber.
layers.expert: The shapes and wall thicknesses are schematic.

title: Right ventricle
summary: The right ventricle pumps oxygen-poor blood to the lungs.

layers.basics: This chamber is shown cut open in the "Inside the heart" view: red for oxygen-rich blood, blue for oxygen-poor.
layers.deeper: Its wall is thinner than the left because the circuit to the lungs is shorter and offers less resistance, so the pressure is lower. The layout is the same as in people. In people: the same chamber.
layers.expert: The shapes and wall thicknesses are schematic.

title: Left atrium
summary: The left atrium receives oxygen-rich blood from the lungs.

layers.basics: This chamber is shown cut open in the "Inside the heart" view: red for oxygen-rich blood, blue for oxygen-poor.
layers.deeper: It passes the blood down to the left ventricle through the mitral valve. The layout is the same as in people. In people: the same chamber.
layers.expert: The shapes and wall thicknesses are schematic.

title: Right atrium
summary: The right atrium receives oxygen-poor blood from the body.

layers.basics: This chamber is shown cut open in the "Inside the heart" view: red for oxygen-rich blood, blue for oxygen-poor.
layers.deeper: Blood from the vena cavae gathers here before it passes through to the right ventricle. The pacemaker (sinoatrial node) is in its wall. The layout is the same as in people. In people: the same chamber.
layers.expert: The shapes and wall thicknesses are schematic.

title: Heart valves
summary: Four valves of thin flaps make the blood go one way: in, through, and out.

layers.basics: The valves open and close with every heartbeat. The "lub-dub" sound is the valves closing.
layers.deeper: The mitral valve (left) and tricuspid valve (right) lie between atrium and ventricle, and the aortic and pulmonary valves lie at the exits. Same set as in people. In older dogs the mitral valve may thicken and leak. In people: the same four valves. Compare the human aortic valve.
layers.expert: The model draws four rings at the approximate positions; they are placeholders for the valves, not valve shapes.

title: Sclera (white of the eye)
summary: The tough white wall of the eyeball.

layers.basics: The sclera is the outer coat of the eye. A dog's sclera shows less white than a person's.
layers.deeper: It is connective tissue that holds the shape of the eye and anchors the muscles that turn it. In people: the same layer; more of it is visible, so the "whites" of the eyes show.
layers.expert: The model draws it as a shell.

title: Choroid (dark layer)
summary: A dark, blood-rich layer behind the retina that feeds it and absorbs stray light.

layers.basics: Under the sensing layer there is a layer full of blood vessels and dark pigment. It nourishes the retina. In the part of the dog's eye below the tapetum, it is dark.
layers.deeper: In the upper part of a dog's eye the tapetum lies in the choroid; in the lower part the choroid is dark and absorbs light. In people: the choroid is dark all the way round; there is no tapetum.
layers.expert: The model shows the dark part only in the lower half.

title: Tapetum lucidum
summary: A shiny layer behind the retina that bounces light back through it for a second chance, so dogs see better in dim light and their eyes glow in a torch beam.

layers.basics: This is something you do not have. Light that passes through the retina without being caught hits the tapetum and is reflected back through the retina for a second chance. That is why dog eyes glow yellow-green in a torch beam or car headlights.
layers.deeper: The tapetum of a dog lies in the upper half of the back of the eye, between the choroid and the retinal pigment layer (it is in the choroid, not in the retina itself). In summaries of the structure it has 9-20 layers of flat, rectangular cells holding zinc-rich rods lined up in parallel. It looks yellow-green in adult dogs and blue in puppies until about four months old. Cats' tapeta contain riboflavin as well as zinc; the dog's rods contain zinc.
layers.expert: In the dog the reflecting rods (rodlets) are about as big as a cat's but more closely packed, which sets the wavelength they reflect best, and they are less precisely lined up than in the cat, which appears to make the reflection less efficient (Lesiuk and Braekevelt 1983). The reflecting layer thins toward the edge of the eye. The tapetum scene is reached with the button on the retina or tapetum card.

facts: typically yellow-green in adults, blue in puppies

ext.title: Fine structure of the canine tapetum lucidum (Lesiuk and Braekevelt 1983, Journal of Anatomy)

title: Retina
summary: The retina is the sheet of light-sensing cells at the back of the eye: many rods for dim light, fewer cones for colour.

layers.basics: The retina turns light into nerve signals. A dog has far more rod cells than cones, so it sees well in dim light, and only two kinds of cone, so its colour world is limited (roughly blue and yellow, with less red-green). Press the button to look at its cells.
layers.deeper: Dog cones peak at about 429 nm (blue) and about 555 nm (green-yellow), so dogs are dichromats, like a person with red-green colour blindness. In the area centralis (the sharpest spot) there are about 23 rods for each cone; in the lower periphery about 41. In people: three cone types (blue, green, red) and a fovea; no tapetum. Compare the human rod cell. Compare the human cone cell.
layers.expert: In a study of the beagle retina cones numbered about 23,000-26,000 per square millimetre at the area centralis and rods about 501,000 per square millimetre. The cone peak sensitivities 429 and 555 nm are from the same study; another source gives 440 and 555 nm.

ext.title: Cone and rod photoreceptors in the beagle retina (Mol Vis 2008)

title: Lens
summary: The lens is a clear disc that fine-tunes the focus of light on the retina.

layers.basics: The cornea does most of the bending of light; the lens adds the finer, adjustable focus.
layers.deeper: The same structure as the human lens.
layers.expert: The model draws a smooth oval.

title: Cornea
summary: The clear front window of the eye.

layers.basics: It lets light in and does most of the focusing. It is kept wet by tears.
layers.deeper: The same as in people. In people: the same part.
layers.expert: The model draws the cornea as a clear cap.

title: Iris and pupil
summary: The coloured ring that opens and closes the pupil to let in more or less light.

layers.basics: The pupil of a dog is round and is a hole, not a coloured part; muscles in the iris change its size.
layers.deeper: Same as in people: round pupil in dogs. In people: the same part.
layers.expert: The model draws the iris and pupil as a ring.

title: Vitreous body
summary: A clear jelly fills the middle of the eyeball and holds the retina in place.

layers.basics: The jelly is mostly water. It keeps the eye round.
layers.deeper: Same as in people. In people: the same.
layers.expert: The model draws it as a transparent ball.

title: Ethmoturbinates (smell lining)
summary: At the back of a dog's nose, thin scrolls of bone folded up like parchment are covered with a smell-sensing lining that is far larger than yours.

layers.basics: Air breathed in flows through the nose; some of it goes to the back where the smell-sensing scrolls are. The folding packs a large surface into a small space. Press the button to look inside the lining.
layers.deeper: The area of a dog's smell lining depends on the breed: about 95-126 cm² is quoted for German shepherds in a 2021 review and about 170 cm² for some dogs, against about 5 cm² (OpenStax) to 10 cm² (Wikipedia) in a person. The number of receptor cells is uncertain: the review gives 200-300 million for dogs, a textbook about 1 billion for most dogs and about 12 million for people. A dog has about 870 intact smell-receptor genes (1,094 genes in the sequenced boxer genome, of which 20.3 % are pseudogenes, broken copies; an earlier estimate was about 1,300 genes). People have about 330-340 intact genes: one paper counted about 900 genes with 63 % pseudogenes, another counted 339 intact genes directly. The dog and human counts come from different genomes and methods, so they are approximate. The folding itself is more intricate in the real nose than the schematic scrolls drawn here. In people: the lining is on the roof of the nose, a patch of about 5 cm² (OpenStax) and the scrolls (turbinates) are small.
layers.expert: Dogs sniff in short bursts, and the nasal passage divides the air into a route for smell and a route to the lungs.

facts: ≈ 95-170 cm² in dogs (varies with breed) vs ≈ 5-10 cm² in a person
≈ 200 million to ≈ 1 billion in dogs (sources differ) vs ≈ 12 million in a person (textbook)

open_questions: How many receptor cells does a dog have? Published estimates differ by a factor of about five (200-300 million in a 2021 review, about 1 billion in a textbook) and are old.

did_you_know: A dog's nose also has a second chemical organ, the vomeronasal organ, above the roof of the mouth, for chemical signals from other animals.

title: Maxilloturbinates (airway lining)
summary: The scrolls at the front of the nose warm, wet and clean the air on its way in.

layers.basics: These scrolls are lined with moist, blood-rich skin. They warm cold air and add moisture, and trap dust and germs on mucus.
layers.deeper: In panting they also give off heat: moisture evaporates from them and cools the blood. This airway lining lies in front of the smell lining and is not itself the sense of smell. In people: the same job done by the nasal conchae.
layers.expert: The shape drawn is a schematic of a much finer structure.

title: Ear canal
summary: A dog's ear canal is L-shaped: down first, then inward to the eardrum.

layers.basics: Sound goes down the vertical part of the canal and then turns inward.
layers.deeper: The canal is lined with skin and wax glands. It has the bend described above. In people the canal is shorter and almost straight. The human explorer has no card for the ear yet.
layers.expert: The model draws a simple bent tube.

title: Eardrum
summary: A thin membrane at the inner end of the ear canal that vibrates with sound.

layers.basics: Sound waves in the canal make the eardrum vibrate. The vibration is passed on to the three tiny bones of the middle ear.
layers.deeper: The same as in people. In people: the same part. The human explorer has no card for the ear yet.
layers.expert: The model draws it as a disc.

facts: turns air pressure waves into vibration

title: Middle ear (bulla)
summary: The middle ear sits in a bony bubble, the bulla, on the underside of the skull.

layers.basics: Three tiny bones carry the vibration from the eardrum to the inner ear. In a dog the cavity is a bulge you can see on the skull from below.
layers.deeper: Same three bones as in people (the hammer, anvil and stirrup). In people: the same chain of three bones; there is no bulla bulge. The human explorer has no card for the ear yet.
layers.expert: The model draws the bubble without the three bones.

title: Cochlea and balance canals
summary: The cochlea is a snail-shaped tube in the skull that turns vibration into nerve signals; next to it, three loops sense turning of the head.

layers.basics: The cochlea holds the hair cells that detect sound. Its different parts react to different pitch. The loops next to it, the semicircular canals, are the balance organ.
layers.deeper: In one comparison table a dog hears from about 67 Hz to about 45 kHz, a wider range than a person (about 64 Hz to 23 kHz on the same criteria). The range depends on the loudness of the test tone and on the individual. In people: the same inner ear, with a narrower range of hearing. The human explorer has no card for the ear yet.
layers.expert: The model draws the snail and the loops at a schematic size.

facts: ≈ 67 Hz to 45 kHz (depends on the test tone and the dog)

title: Inside a dog's skin and coat
summary: A slice through the skin shows the thin outer layer, the thick dermis, the fat below, and the hair follicles that grow the double coat.

layers.basics: This is a schematic drawn from what is known about how dog skin is built. Hair roots sit in the dermis; a thick guard hair and a tuft of finer hairs leave through the same opening. Click a layer to read about it.
layers.deeper: The skin has three layers: a thin epidermis on top, the dermis with the follicles and glands, and fatty tissue below. A dog's follicles are compound: one big hair and a tuft of smaller ones share one opening. In people: the same three layers.
layers.expert: Every size in the scene is illustrative. What is real is the arrangement of the layers, the compound follicles and the types of gland.

title: Epidermis and the skin barrier
summary: The outer skin is a thin layer of cells that die and flatten into a waterproof barrier.

layers.basics: Cells are made at the bottom of the epidermis and move up as they fill with keratin and die. The top layer, the stratum corneum, is like roof tiles glued with fat. This keeps water in and germs out.
layers.deeper: The glue between the dead cells is a mixture of lipids: ceramides, cholesterol and free fatty acids. In dogs with atopic dermatitis these lipids are reduced. Press the button to see one of them, cholesterol. In people: the same layers and the same kind of lipids. Compare the human keratinocyte.
layers.expert: Dog stratum corneum lipid levels have been measured in atopic and healthy dogs; this card quotes only the composition, not amounts.

title: Dermis
summary: The dermis is the tough, flexible layer under the epidermis that holds the follicles, glands, blood vessels and nerves.

layers.basics: It is made mostly of collagen fibres. It gives the skin strength and holds the hair roots.
layers.deeper: The same tissue as in people. In people: the same layer.
layers.expert: Not drawn in detail.

title: Compound hair follicle
summary: One opening, many hairs: a dog's follicle grows a thick guard hair and a tuft of fine undercoat hairs together.

layers.basics: In a Labrador the hairs come out in small groups. The big one (the guard hair) sheds water; the fine ones make a warm, soft felt.
layers.deeper: Each follicle has a root bulb where cells divide, a sebaceous gland that oils the hair, and an apocrine sweat gland. The follicle cycles between growth, rest and shedding. A central hair is surrounded by about 3-15 smaller hairs, all leaving through one pore.
layers.expert: All the hairs of one follicle leave through a common pore.

ext.title: The integumentary system in animals (Merck Veterinary Manual)

title: Undercoat
summary: The undercoat is the soft, fine layer of hair under the guard hairs.

layers.basics: It traps a layer of air, so it insulates. Dogs shed it in cycles.
layers.deeper: These are the secondary hairs of each compound follicle.
layers.expert: Not drawn separately on the model.

title: Skin glands
summary: Two kinds of gland open into the follicles: oil glands and sweat glands of the apocrine type. The other kind of sweat gland, the one people cool with, is found only on the paw pads.

layers.basics: The oil from sebaceous glands waterproofs hair. Apocrine (epitrichial) sweat glands are attached to the follicles over the body. The paw pads have the other kind of sweat gland, which opens straight onto the skin.
layers.deeper: A dog does have sweat glands in the body skin: apocrine (also called epitrichial) glands lie with the hair follicles, while the other kind (atrichial; people have this kind all over their skin) is present only on the paw pads. Some clinical evidence suggests that limited sweating occurs in dogs and may play a minor part in cooling; dogs cool mainly by panting and drooling. In people: sweat glands all over the skin of the atrichial (eccrine) kind are the main way people cool.
layers.expert: The gland sizes and positions are schematic.

title: Inside the smell lining
summary: A slice of the smell lining: sensing cells reach to the surface with tiny hairs that catch odour molecules, held up by supporting cells.

layers.basics: Smell cells are nerve cells. Each has a tuft of hair-like cilia in the mucus at the surface. When an odour molecule fits a receptor on a cilium, the cell sends a signal along its thread (the axon) to the brain. Click a part.
layers.deeper: The lining has three kinds of cell: smell neurons, supporting cells and stem cells at the bottom that replace the neurons. The glands in the layer below make the mucus. In people: the same layers on a smaller patch.
layers.expert: All sizes are illustrative. The layers and cell types are as in a mammal's smell lining.

facts: smell neurons, supporting cells, basal (stem) cells

title: Olfactory sensory neuron
summary: A smell cell is a nerve cell that senses odour molecules with receptors on its cilia and sends the signal to the brain.

layers.basics: Each smell cell carries one type of receptor. Odour molecules dissolve in the mucus, fit a receptor and trigger a signal. Press the button to see the molecule that carries the message inside the cell.
layers.deeper: When an odour binds the receptor, the receptor activates a G protein that turns on an enzyme (adenylyl cyclase). The enzyme makes cyclic AMP (cAMP) from ATP, cAMP opens channels in the cilium that let calcium and sodium in, and the cell fires. A dog has about 870 intact receptor genes and a person about 330-340 (see the Turbinates card for where these counts come from and how uncertain they are). In people: the same type of neuron.
layers.expert: Smell cells are replaced throughout life from the stem cells at the base of the lining. Each cell expresses one receptor gene out of the many; how a cell chooses one is a research question.

facts: ≈ 870 intact genes in the dog (1,094 genes, 20.3 % pseudogenes; Quignon 2005) against ≈ 330-340 in a person (≈ 900 genes with 63 % pseudogenes, Quignon 2003; 339 intact genes counted directly, Malnic 2004). The counts come from different genomes and methods.
open_questions: How does each smell cell pick just one of its several hundred receptor genes? This is still being studied.
